title: Linux CFS (Completely Fair Scheduler)
summary: CFS is the default Linux CPU scheduler. It uses a red-black tree ordered by vruntime (virtual runtime). Each task's vruntime increases at a rate inversely proportional to its weight (priority). The scheduler picks the task with the smallest vruntime. Nice values (-20 to +19) map to weights (higher nice = lower weight = less CPU). CFS aims to give each task a fair share of CPU time.

structure.meaning: Virtual runtime: accumulated CPU time weighted by priority. Lower = higher priority.
Task weight (from nice value). Higher weight = more CPU time. nice -20 = weight 88761, nice 0 = 1024, nice +19 = 15.
Red-black tree ordered by vruntime. The leftmost node is the next task to run.
Target latency: the period in which every runnable task should get at least one time slice.
nice -20..+19 maps to weights via a lookup table (sched_prio_to_weight). Each nice level is ~10% CPU difference.
cgroup v2 CPU controller: cpu.max = 'quota period' (e.g., '100000 100000' = 1 CPU). Throttles tasks exceeding the quota.

notes: CFS replaced the O(1) scheduler in Linux 2.6.23.
CFS is O(log n) per scheduling decision (red-black tree).
Real-time scheduling: SCHED_FIFO (first-in-first-out) and SCHED_RR (round-robin) for real-time tasks.
Deadline scheduling: SCHED_DEADLINE (earliest deadline first) for real-time tasks.
CFS uses vruntime to ensure fairness: higher-priority tasks accumulate vruntime slower.
